MovieScript:
High noon at Sad Hill Cemetery. The sun was a physical weight, pressing down on the vast, circular wasteland of the dead. Thousands of wooden crosses, weathered and gray, stood like a silent army under the relentless glare. The only sound was the wind, a low, mournful howl that whipped the yellow dust across the parched earth.

In the center of the clearing, Tuco was a man possessed. Drenched in sweat, his clothes caked in the grime of a dozen deserts, he knelt inside the open grave of "Arch Stanton." He wasn't using a shovel; he was clawing at the earth with a jagged piece of wood, his breath coming in ragged, desperate gasps. He struck wood. With a guttural cry, he smashed the lid of the casket open.

There was no gold. There was only a skeleton, its jaw unhinged in a perpetual, hollow grin.

Tuco stared at the bleached bones, his face contorting. "There’s no name!" he croaked, his voice cracking with a mix of fury and exhaustion. "There’s nothing here!"

A long, sharp shadow fell across the grave. Tuco froze.

Angel Eyes stood at the edge of the pit, looking down like an angel of death. He was motionless, his Remington revolver held with a terrifying, steady grace. The black bore of the gun pointed directly at Tuco’s heart. A few paces behind him, leaning casually against a stone, was Blondie. He looked as if he were merely waiting for a train, his iconic poncho draped over his shoulders, a thin trail of cigar smoke drifting from his lips into the heat-shimmered air.

"Two can dig a lot quicker than one," Angel Eyes said, his voice as cold as a cellar floor. He kicked a shovel toward the grave. "Dig."

Blondie didn't even glance at the shovel. He kept the cigar firmly between his teeth, his squinted eyes tracking the movement of the clouds. For twenty seconds, the world stopped. The only movement was the swaying of the grass and the slow flap of Blondie’s poncho.

"You’d better not dig," Blondie said, his voice a low, gravelly rasp. "If you shoot me, you’ll never see a cent of that money."

The silence sharpened. Angel Eyes slowly thumbed back the hammer of his pistol. Click. The sound was as loud as a gunshot in the stillness. He shifted his aim, the barrel now centered on Blondie’s chest.

"Why?" Angel Eyes asked.

Blondie took the cigar from his mouth with agonizing slowness. He turned his head, meeting Angel Eyes’ icy stare with a gaze that was just as lethal. "I’ll tell you why. Because there’s nothing in there."

Tuco scrambled out of the grave, his eyes darting between the two men like a trapped animal. He looked at the gun, then at Blondie, his chest heaving. "You son of a..." he hissed, his fingers twitching near his empty holster. "You think I’m going to believe you?"

Blondie ignored him completely. His world had narrowed down to the man with the Remington. "Two hundred thousand dollars is a lot of money," Blondie said calmly. "We’re going to have to earn it."

Angel Eyes narrowed his eyes, his gun hand like a rock. "How?"

Without a word, Blondie reached into the folds of his poncho. Both Angel Eyes and Tuco went rigid, their nerves frayed to the breaking point. But Blondie didn't draw a gun. He pulled out a smooth, flat stone and held it up for them to see.

"I’ll write the real name on the bottom of this rock," Blondie said.

He bent down, moving with the deliberate caution of a man walking on glass. He placed the stone face-down in the exact center of the vast, circular stone plaza. Then, he began to back away. Step by step. Slowly.

Angel Eyes watched the stone for a moment, then slowly lowered his revolver. He too began to retreat, moving toward the opposite edge of the circle. Tuco, sensing the shift in the air, stumbled backward toward the third point of the compass.

They stopped.

Three men. A perfect, deadly triangle on the scorched stone floor. The wind died down, leaving a vacuum of silence. The camera of the mind jumped from one face to the other: Angel Eyes’ cold calculation, Tuco’s frantic desperation, and Blondie’s unshakable calm. Their hands hovered over their holsters, fingers poised like spiders. Under the burning sun, the standoff stretched out, a long, breathless moment where life and death hung by a single, invisible thread.
